decks.title: Concepts of Cost — Part 1: Kinds of Cost and Total Costs
goals: Distinguish explicit and implicit, private and social, money and real costs
Explain opportunity cost and compare accounting and economic profit
Distinguish fixed and variable costs and describe the total cost curves

slides.heading: Concepts of Cost
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **kinds of cost** an economist counts, **opportunity cost**, and the **total cost curves** of the short run.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: explicit and implicit cost, private and social cost, money, real and economic cost, opportunity cost, fixed and variable cost, and the total cost curves
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A bakery, a dyeing unit and a farmer all face costs. But an accountant and an economist do not count cost in the same way. In this part we sort costs into kinds, meet the idea of opportunity cost, and then look at how total cost changes with output in the short run.

slides.heading: Explicit and implicit costs
columns: **Explicit costs** are **actual payments** to outsiders: wages, raw materials, rent paid to a landlord.
**Implicit costs** are the **imputed value** of the owner's **own** factors: her own shop, savings and time.

rows: Imputed value of the owner's own factors
Rent of her own shop, her forgone salary

visual.alt: Table comparing explicit and implicit costs: explicit costs are payments to outsiders and appear in the books; implicit costs are the imputed value of the owner's own factors and are counted by economists but not by accountants

slides.narration: Some costs are paid out in money to other people. These are explicit costs, and they appear in the account books. Others are the value of things the owner supplies herself, such as her own shop or her own time. No payment is made, so accountants leave them out, but economists count them as implicit costs.

slides.heading: Quick check: what counts as economic cost?
slides.body_md: For an economist judging an imagined Indore sweet shop, economic cost equals…
slides.narration: Think about both kinds of cost you have just met. Does the economist leave either of them out?

slides.heading: Private and social cost
slides.body_md: **Social cost = private cost + external cost** borne by others who are not paid for it.

nodes.label: Private cost borne by the firm
External cost borne by others (pollution, noise, congestion)
Social cost to society as a whole

visual.alt: Flow showing social cost as the private cost borne by the firm plus the external cost it imposes on others such as pollution, noise or congestion
visual.caption: Imagined Pali dyeing unit: ₹4,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹5,50,000

slides.narration: A firm counts only the costs it bears itself: its private cost. But its production may harm others, for example through polluted water or smoke. That harm is an external cost. Add it to the private cost and you get the social cost, the full cost to society of producing the good.

slides.heading: Money, real and economic cost

rows: Rupee spending on inputs and hired factors
Toil, risk and sacrifice of factor owners
The family's nights at the boiling pans
Payments plus the family's forgone income

visual.alt: Table of money cost, real cost and economic cost with examples from an imagined jaggery unit: rupee spending, the toil and sacrifice of the people involved, and explicit plus implicit costs

slides.narration: Money cost is what is spent in rupees. Real cost is the effort, risk and sacrifice of the people who supply the factors, like a family working through the night at a jaggery unit. Economic cost adds together the payments made and the value of the owners' own factors, the explicit and implicit costs.

slides.heading: Opportunity cost
slides.body_md:
**Opportunity cost** is the value of the **next best alternative given up**.

- Only the **best** forgone use counts, not all of them added up.
- If a resource has **no other use**, its opportunity cost is **zero**.

nodes.label: Next best use given up is the opportunity cost

visual.alt: Flow showing that a scarce resource has several possible uses; choosing one means giving up the next best use, which is the opportunity cost
visual.caption: Every choice has a forgone alternative

slides.narration: Resources are scarce, so using them one way means not using them another way. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up. Notice the word best. We do not add up every alternative. And if something truly has no other use, choosing it costs nothing in this sense.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a farmer's choice
slides.body_md: An imagined Vidarbha farmer can grow **cotton**, grow **soybean** or **lease** his land for the season. What is the opportunity cost of growing cotton?
bullets: Step 1 — List the alternatives and their incomes.
Step 2 — Leave out the chosen one (cotton).
Step 3 — Pick the highest remaining income: soybean.

headers: Use of the land for one season

visual.alt: Worked example: an imagined Vidarbha farmer can earn 80,000 rupees from cotton, 65,000 from soybean or 50,000 from leasing; the opportunity cost of cotton is the next best alternative, 65,000
visual.caption: Opportunity cost of cotton = next best alternative = ₹65,000

slides.narration: Write down every use of the land and what it would earn. Cotton is the choice, so set it aside. Of the remaining two, soybean pays more than leasing. So the opportunity cost of cotton is the soybean income of sixty-five thousand rupees, not the two alternatives added together.

slides.heading: Quick check: is opportunity cost always money?
slides.body_md: True or false: opportunity cost exists only when the alternative given up can be measured in money.
slides.narration: Think of a student who gives up an afternoon of rest. Is anything given up even if no money changes hands?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: accounting and economic profit
slides.body_md: An imagined Kozhikode bakery: does the owner really profit after counting what she gives up?
bullets: Step 1 — Accounting profit = revenue − explicit costs.
Step 2 — Add up implicit costs: forgone salary and rent.
Step 3 — Economic profit = accounting profit − implicit costs.

visual.alt: Worked example for an imagined Kozhikode bakery: accounting profit 55,000 rupees, implicit costs 50,000, economic profit 5,000
visual.caption: Imagined figures: economic profit = accounting profit − implicit costs.

slides.narration: The bakery takes in two lakh forty thousand rupees a month and pays out one lakh eighty-five thousand, so the accountant sees a profit of fifty-five thousand. But the owner gives up a salary and the rent of her own shop, fifty thousand together. Her economic profit is only five thousand rupees: still positive, but small.

slides.heading: Fixed and variable costs
columns: **Fixed costs** do **not change** with output and must be paid even at **zero** output: rent, loan interest, salaried staff.
**Variable costs** **change** with output and are zero when nothing is produced: raw materials, power, daily wages.

rows: Shed rent, loan interest, manager's salary

visual.alt: Table comparing fixed and variable costs: fixed costs do not change with output and are paid even at zero output; variable costs change with output and are zero when nothing is produced; in the long run all costs are variable

slides.narration: In the short run some factors cannot be changed quickly, such as the plant itself. Their costs are fixed: they stay the same whatever the output and must be paid even if the plant stands idle. Other costs rise and fall with output. These are variable costs, and they are zero when nothing is produced.

slides.heading: Total fixed, variable and total cost
slides.body_md: **TC = TFC + TVC**. TFC is flat; TVC starts at the **origin**; TC starts at the **TFC level** and runs **parallel** to TVC.

slides.narration: Average fixed cost is fixed cost per unit. With a fixed cost of one hundred and twenty, it is sixty at an output of two, thirty at four and fifteen at eight. It keeps falling, but since the fixed cost never disappears, it never reaches zero. Such a curve is called a rectangular hyperbola.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Payments made vs value of own factors
Value of the next best alternative
Fixed at zero output; variable changes with output
TC = TFC + TVC; TFC flat, TVC from the origin

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: explicit and implicit costs, private and social costs, opportunity cost, fixed and variable costs, and the total cost curves

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Explicit costs are payments made; implicit costs are the value of the owner's own factors. Social cost adds external harm to private cost. Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up. In the short run, fixed costs stay the same and variable costs change with output, and total cost is their sum.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always give an **example** with each cost concept; tie it to the firm named in the question.
Opportunity cost = **next best** alternative only, never the sum of all alternatives.
Economic profit = accounting profit − **implicit costs**; show both figures.
TFC is **horizontal**, TVC starts at the **origin**, TC starts at **TFC** and stays parallel to TVC.
AFC is a **rectangular hyperbola**: it never touches the output axis.
slides.narration: Examiners reward examples, so attach one to every concept. In opportunity cost questions, pick only the best alternative. When asked about profit, show the accounting figure and then subtract the implicit costs. When you draw total cost curves, check where each one starts. And remember that average fixed cost never reaches zero.

decks.title: Concepts of Cost — Part 2: Average and Marginal Costs, Short Run and Long Run
goals: Calculate AFC, AVC, AC and MC from a cost schedule
Explain the relationships among MC, AVC and AC and the narrowing gap between AC and AVC
Describe the long-run average cost curve as an envelope of short-run curves (concepts only)

slides.heading: Concepts of Cost, Part 2
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **average** and **marginal** costs, how they are related, and **short-run** versus **long-run** cost curves.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: average costs, marginal cost, completing a schedule, the link between marginal and average cost, the U-shapes, and long-run costs
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Total cost tells us how much a whole batch costs. Firms also want to know the cost per unit and the cost of one more unit. In this part we work out average and marginal costs, see how they are linked, and then compare costs in the short run with costs in the long run.

slides.heading: Average and marginal costs

rows: Starts at TFC; parallel to TVC
U-shaped, minimum to the right of AVC

visual.alt: Table of short-run cost formulas and shapes: total cost is fixed plus variable cost; average fixed cost is fixed cost over output; average variable cost is variable cost over output; average cost is total cost over output; marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit

slides.narration: Average fixed cost is fixed cost per unit. Average variable cost is variable cost per unit, and average cost is total cost per unit, which equals the two averages added. Marginal cost is different: it is the extra cost of producing one more unit, found as the change in total cost, or equally the change in variable cost.

slides.heading: Quick check: meaning of marginal cost
slides.body_md: Marginal cost is the…
slides.narration: Is it a cost per unit of all units, or the cost of just one extra unit?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: completing a schedule
slides.body_md: An imagined Guntur pickle kitchen has a fixed cost of ₹60 a day. Complete its schedule from total cost.
bullets: Step 1 — TVC = TC − 60.
Step 2 — AFC = 60 ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q, AC = TC ÷ Q.
Step 3 — MC = TC of this output − TC of the previous output.

visual.alt: Completed cost schedule of an imagined Guntur pickle kitchen with a fixed cost of 60 rupees: total costs 60, 100, 130, 150, 180, 230 for 0 to 5 jars, with total variable, average fixed, average variable, average and marginal costs worked out
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ a day.

slides.narration: Start by removing the fixed cost of sixty from each total cost to get variable cost. Divide by output to get the averages. For marginal cost, subtract the previous total cost. Notice that marginal cost falls to twenty at the third jar, equals average variable cost at the fourth, and then jumps to fifty.

The gap between average cost and average variable cost narrows as output rises
visual.caption: Imagined figures: MC turns up first, then cuts AVC and AC at their lowest points.

slides.narration: Here are the four curves for the mug unit. Average fixed cost falls all the way. Marginal cost falls first and turns up at an output of four. It then cuts average variable cost at its lowest point, A, at six, and later cuts average cost at its lowest point, B, a little beyond seven.

slides.heading: The marginal–average rule
slides.body_md: An average is pulled **towards** the marginal value.

visual.alt: Table of the marginal–average rule: when marginal cost is below an average, the average falls; when equal, the average is at its minimum; when above, the average rises
visual.caption: The rule holds for both AVC and AC.

slides.narration: Think of a batting average. If your next score is below your average, the average falls. If it is above, the average rises. If it is equal, the average stays the same. Costs follow the same rule. So marginal cost must pass through the lowest point of average variable cost and of average cost.

slides.heading: Quick check: can AC fall while MC rises?
slides.body_md: True or false: average cost can be falling at an output where marginal cost has already started rising.
slides.narration: Remember the rule: what matters is whether marginal cost is below or above the average, not whether it is rising.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: costs from average variable cost
slides.body_md: An imagined Moradabad bell workshop has a fixed cost of ₹90. From AVC, find TVC, TC and MC.
bullets: Step 1 — TVC = AVC × Q.
Step 2 — TC = 90 + TVC.
Step 3 — MC = change in TVC.
Step 4 — Check: MC below AVC as AVC falls, above it as AVC rises.

visual.alt: Cost schedule of an imagined Moradabad bell workshop with a fixed cost of 90 rupees: from average variable costs 30, 25, 22, 24 the variable costs, total costs and marginal costs follow
visual.caption: Imagined figures: TVC from AVC × Q, then MC.

slides.narration: Multiply each average variable cost by output to get variable cost: thirty, fifty, sixty-six and ninety-six. Add the fixed cost of ninety to get total cost. Marginal cost is the change in variable cost. The fourth bell costs thirty, more than the average of twenty-two, which is why average variable cost rises at four bells.

slides.heading: Why AC and AVC come closer
slides.body_md: AC − AVC = **AFC**. As AFC falls, the two curves **approach** each other, but they **never meet**.

visual.alt: Part of the cost schedule of an imagined Khurja mug unit for outputs 3 to 8 hundred mugs: average variable cost falls to 24 at output 6 and then rises, while marginal cost is below it before output 6 and above it after
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ hundred.

slides.narration: The vertical gap between average cost and average variable cost is average fixed cost. Since average fixed cost keeps falling as output rises, the two curves come closer and closer. But fixed cost never vanishes in the short run, so the gap never closes and the curves never meet.

slides.heading: Quick check: which minimum comes first?
slides.body_md: For the Khurja mug unit, MC is lowest at Q = 4, AVC at Q = 6 and AC at about Q = 7.2. Which statement explains this order?
slides.narration: An average keeps falling as long as the marginal value stays below it. Which curve must turn up first?

slides.heading: Why the short-run curves are U-shaped
bullets: **AVC and MC** fall at first because of **increasing returns** to the variable factor, then rise because of **diminishing returns**: the **law of variable proportions**.
**AC = AFC + AVC** falls while both fall, and rises once the **rise in AVC outweighs the fall in AFC**.

visual.alt: Part of the cost schedule of an imagined Khurja mug unit for outputs 3 to 8 hundred mugs: average variable cost falls to 24 at output 6 and then rises, while marginal cost is below it before output 6 and above it after
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ hundred.

slides.narration: With the plant fixed, adding workers at first raises output fast, so each unit costs less. Later, crowding sets in and each extra unit costs more. This is the law of variable proportions, and it gives average variable cost and marginal cost their U-shape. Average cost turns up later, because falling fixed cost per unit holds it down for a while.

slides.heading: Short run and long run
columns: **Short run:** at least one factor, usually the **plant**, is **fixed**; costs are fixed and variable.
**Long run:** **every** factor can change; **all costs are variable**; the firm chooses its plant size.

rows: LAC: flatter U, envelope of SACs

visual.alt: Table comparing the short run and the long run: in the short run at least one factor and some costs are fixed and the average cost curve is a steeper U because of the law of variable proportions; in the long run all costs are variable and the long-run average cost curve is a flatter U, the envelope of short-run curves, because of economies and diseconomies of scale

slides.narration: The short run is too short to change the size of the plant, so some costs stay fixed. In the long run the firm can build a larger or smaller plant, so every cost becomes variable and there is no fixed cost at all. The reasons for the shapes of the curves are different in each period.

slides.heading: The long-run average cost curve: an envelope
slides.body_md: Each plant size has its own **SAC**. The **LAC** touches each SAC from **below** and wraps around them: the **envelope** or **planning** curve. (Concept only; no derivation.)

visual.alt: Schematic diagram of three U-shaped short-run average cost curves, one for each plant size, and a flatter U-shaped long-run average cost curve below them that touches each short-run curve at one point. The long-run curve wraps around the short-run curves like an envelope
visual.caption: Concept only (no derivation): the LAC is the envelope of the SACs.

slides.narration: Each plant size gives its own short-run average cost curve. In the long run the firm picks, for each output it plans, the plant that gives the lowest cost. The long-run curve joins these lowest costs and touches each short-run curve from below, like an envelope around them. It is flatter than any single short-run curve.

slides.heading: Quick check: costs in long-run planning
slides.body_md: An imagined Haryana dairy can change its plant, land and staff over five years. In this long-run planning…
slides.narration: If every factor can be changed, is any cost still fixed?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: AFC falls; AVC and AC U-shaped
Change in TC from one more unit
MC cuts AVC and AC at their minima
All costs variable; LAC envelopes SACs

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: average costs, marginal cost, the rule linking marginal and average cost, the gap between average cost and average variable cost, and long-run costs

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Average fixed cost always falls, while average variable cost, average cost and marginal cost are U-shaped. Marginal cost turns up first and cuts both averages at their lowest points. The gap between average cost and average variable cost is average fixed cost. In the long run every cost is variable, and the long-run curve envelopes the short-run curves.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In schedules, write the **formula** before each column; MC uses the **previous** total cost.
Given AVC, find TVC = AVC × Q first; given MC, add MCs to get TVC.
Say **why** MC cuts AVC and AC at their minima, not only that it does.
AC and AVC **never meet**: their gap is AFC.
Long-run curves: **concepts only**; give economies and diseconomies of scale as the reason, not fixed costs.
slides.narration: In numerical questions, show the formula for each column so method marks are safe, and remember that marginal cost uses the previous total. If you are given averages or marginals, rebuild total variable cost first. For diagrams, explain the marginal and average rule. And for the long run, describe the envelope idea without trying to derive it.

sections.heading: 1. Kinds of cost
sections.body_md:
- **Explicit cost:** payment to outsiders (wages, materials, rent paid).
- **Implicit cost:** imputed value of the owner's own factors (own shop, savings, time); not in the books.
- **Economic cost** = explicit + implicit.
- **Money cost:** rupee spending. **Real cost:** toil, risk and sacrifice of factor owners.
- **Private cost:** cost borne by the firm. **Social cost** = private cost + **external cost** imposed on others.

key_terms.definition_md: The imputed value of factors owned and supplied by the firm's owner, for which no payment is made.
The total cost to society of producing a good: private cost plus external cost.

sections.heading: 2. Opportunity cost; accounting and economic profit
sections.body_md:
**Opportunity cost** = value of the **next best alternative** forgone. A resource with no alternative use has zero opportunity cost.

**Accounting profit** = revenue − explicit costs. **Economic profit** = accounting profit − implicit costs. A firm can show an accounting profit yet make an economic loss.

key_terms.definition_md: The value of the next best alternative given up when a resource is used in a particular way.
Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs.

sections.body_md:
**TFC:** does not change with output; horizontal line; paid even at zero output.

**TVC:** zero at zero output; rises first at a decreasing rate, then at an increasing rate.

**TC = TFC + TVC:** same shape as TVC, starting at the TFC level; the vertical gap TC − TVC = TFC is constant.

Cost that varies directly with output and is zero at zero output.

sections.heading: 5. Relationships among MC, AVC and AC
sections.body_md:
- MC below an average → the average **falls**; MC equal → average at its **minimum**; MC above → average **rises**.
- MC therefore cuts **AVC** and **AC** at their **lowest points**; MC reaches its own minimum **first**, then AVC, then AC.
- AC − AVC = AFC, so the curves **approach** each other but **never meet**.
- U-shapes in the short run come from the **law of variable proportions**.

sections.heading: 6. Short-run and long-run cost curves (concepts only)
sections.body_md:
In the **long run** all factors are variable, so **all costs are variable** and there is no AFC.

Each plant size has its own **SAC**. The **LAC** shows the lowest average cost of each output when the best plant is chosen; it touches every SAC from below and is called the **envelope** or **planning curve**. It is **flatter** than any SAC and U-shaped because of **economies** and then **diseconomies of scale**. (Derivation of the curves is not required.)

key_terms.definition_md: The long-run average cost curve, which touches each short-run average cost curve from below.
Savings in average cost from a larger scale of production.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Adding all alternatives to find opportunity cost instead of taking the next best.
- Leaving implicit costs out when asked for economic profit.
- Starting the TC curve at the origin, or drawing TFC as rising.
- Computing MC as TC ÷ Q, or subtracting the next total cost instead of the previous one.
- Saying AFC becomes zero, or that AC and AVC meet.
- Explaining the U-shape of the long-run AC by fixed costs.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option, value or term.
- 2 marks: definition with an example, or formula and answer.
- 3 marks: working for several values, or three explained points.
- 5 marks: parts answered in order, with completed schedules or described diagrams and reasons.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Nagpur printing press pays ₹18,000 a month as rent for its hall to a landlord. For the press this payment is

options.text_md: an implicit cost
an explicit cost
a social cost only
a sunk opportunity with no cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an explicit cost. A payment actually made to an outsider for a factor is an explicit (accounting) cost. An implicit cost is the value of the owner's own factor, for which no payment is made.

questions.stem_md: A tailor in an imagined Bhopal market runs her business in a shop she owns and could otherwise rent out for ₹9,000 a month. In economics the ₹9,000 is

options.text_md: an explicit cost entered in her cash book
not a cost at all, because no money is paid
part of the social cost borne by her neighbours
an implicit cost of her business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an implicit cost of her business. She gives up the rent she could have earned, so the ₹9,000 is the imputed value of her own factor: an implicit cost. It is not paid out, so it is not in her cash book, but economists still count it.

questions.stem_md: Coloured waste from an imagined dyeing unit in Pali makes river water unfit for the farms downstream. The loss suffered by those farmers is part of

options.text_md: the social cost of the unit's output
the private cost paid by the unit
the implicit cost of the unit's owner
the fixed cost of the unit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the social cost of the unit's output. Social cost is the total cost to society: the firm's private cost plus costs it imposes on others without paying, such as the farmers' loss. The unit does not pay that loss, so it is not part of its private cost.

questions.stem_md: The tiredness, risk and sacrifice of leisure borne by the workers and owners of an imagined Agra marble-inlay workshop are together called its

options.text_md: money cost of production
explicit cost of production
real cost of production
marginal cost of production

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** real cost of production. Real cost is the pains and sacrifices of the factor owners in producing the good; money cost is the expenditure in rupees on factors and inputs.

questions.stem_md: For an economist judging an imagined Indore sweet shop, the economic cost of running it equals

options.text_md: explicit costs only
implicit costs only
explicit costs plus implicit costs
the social cost minus the private cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** explicit costs plus implicit costs. Economic cost includes the payments made to outsiders (explicit) and the value of the owner's own factors (implicit), such as his own labour, capital and premises.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The social cost of electricity from an imagined coal-fired plant near Korba can exceed the plant's private cost.

**Reason (R):** Social cost adds to private cost the harm the plant's smoke causes to nearby residents, for which the plant pays nothing.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the external harm is added to the private cost, so social cost is larger whenever such harm exists.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The salary a shop-owner forgoes by working in his own shop is entered as an expense in the shop's account books.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** An implicit cost involves no payment, so accountants do not record it; economists add it when they measure economic cost and economic profit.

questions.stem_md: Private cost plus the external cost a firm imposes on others gives the ___ cost of production.
questions.solution_md: Social cost = private cost + external cost borne by the rest of society.

questions.stem_md: Match each cost of an imagined Shillong tea café with the type of cost it illustrates.

options.text_md: Wages paid to two waiters
Interest the owner could earn on her own savings used in the café
Litter from takeaway cups cleaned up by the municipality
The owner's long hours and stress

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Wages are paid out (explicit); forgone interest on own savings is imputed (implicit); litter cleared by the town is borne by others (external, adding to social cost); toil and stress are a real cost.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between explicit and implicit costs, giving one example of each for an imagined photocopy shop in Patna.
questions.solution_md: Each defined with a Patna example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Explicit** costs are **actual payments** to outsiders for factors and inputs, such as the **paper and toner** the Patna shop buys. **Implicit** costs are the **imputed value of the owner's own factors**, such as the **salary he gives up** to run the shop himself.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Pali dyeing unit spends ₹4,00,000 a month on production, and its waste water causes crop losses of ₹1,50,000 a month to farmers downstream. Find the social cost and explain why it differs from the private cost.
questions.solution_md: ₹5,50,000, with the external cost explained.

answer.model_answer_md: **Social cost = private cost + external cost = ₹4,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹5,50,000** a month. It is higher because the farmers' loss is a cost **to society** that the unit **does not pay**.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: external cost not paid by the firm

questions.stem_md: Explain money cost, real cost and economic cost, using an imagined family-run jaggery unit near Kolhapur as your example.
questions.solution_md: Three concepts, each with a jaggery-unit example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Money cost** is the **rupee expenditure** on inputs and hired factors, such as cane, fuel and wages paid to helpers.
2. **Real cost** is the **toil, risk and sacrifice** of the people involved, such as the family's long nights at the boiling pans.
3. **Economic cost** adds the **implicit costs** of the family's own land, labour and savings to the explicit money payments.

questions.stem_md: An imagined family runs a rice mill near Thanjavur on its own land, using its own savings and labour, and hires two operators. Explain five concepts of cost with reference to the mill.
questions.solution_md: Five concepts tied to the mill.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Explicit cost:** wages paid to the **two operators**, electricity and paddy bought are **actual payments** to outsiders.
2. **Implicit cost:** the **rent** the family could earn by leasing its land, the **interest** on its savings and the **salary** it could earn elsewhere are imputed costs of its own factors.
3. **Economic cost:** explicit plus implicit costs; only when revenue covers this do the owners earn more than in their best alternative.
4. **Private versus social cost:** if husk smoke harms neighbours, the social cost exceeds the mill's private cost by that external harm.
5. **Real cost:** the **toil and risk** borne by the family and operators in running the mill.

questions.stem_md: Opportunity cost of using a resource in one way is best described as

options.text_md: the value of the next best alternative given up
the total of all alternatives given up
the money price paid for the resource
the cost borne by society because of pollution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the value of the next best alternative given up. Only the best forgone alternative counts, not all alternatives added together; the price paid may differ from what is given up.

questions.stem_md: For one season an imagined Vidarbha farmer can earn ₹80,000 from cotton, ₹65,000 from soybean, or ₹50,000 by leasing his land. If he grows cotton, its opportunity cost is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹65,000. The next best alternative given up is soybean at ₹65,000, which is more than the lease income; the sum of all alternatives is not the opportunity cost.

questions.stem_md: An old storeroom in an imagined Kalimpong school has no other use: nobody would rent it and the school cannot use it for anything else. When the school starts storing library books there, the opportunity cost of the room is

options.text_md: equal to the rent of a similar room in the town
zero, as nothing is given up
equal to the cost of building a new room
equal to the value of the books stored

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** zero, as nothing is given up. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone. If the room has no alternative use, nothing is sacrificed and the opportunity cost is zero.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Vidarbha farmer can earn ₹80,000 from cotton, ₹65,000 from soybean or ₹50,000 from leasing his land for the season. What is the opportunity cost (in ₹) of growing cotton?
questions.solution_md: Next best alternative: soybean, ₹65,000 (greater than the lease of ₹50,000). Opportunity cost = ₹65,000.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Kozhikode bakery earns revenue of ₹2,40,000 a month and pays explicit costs of ₹1,85,000. Its owner gives up a salary of ₹40,000 and the rent of ₹10,000 she could earn on her shop. Find the bakery's economic profit (in ₹) for the month.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Accounting profit = 2,40,000 − 1,85,000 = 55,000.
Step 2: Implicit costs = 40,000 + 10,000 = 50,000.
Step 3: Economic profit = 55,000 − 50,000 = 5,000.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A firm can show an accounting profit and still make an economic loss.

**Reason (R):** Accounting cost is recorded from bills and payments made during the year.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. A holds because economic cost also includes implicit costs (the owner's forgone salary, rent and interest); if these exceed the accounting profit, there is an economic loss. R merely says how accounting cost is recorded.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Opportunity cost exists only when the alternative given up can be measured in money.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone, which may be leisure, time or another good; money is only a convenient measure of it.

questions.stem_md: Define opportunity cost and illustrate it with an imagined Class 12 student in Ranchi who spends Sunday afternoons in a paid coaching class.
questions.solution_md: Definition and a specific forgone alternative.

answer.model_answer_md: The **opportunity cost** of a choice is **what the best rejected option was worth**. If the Ranchi student's next best use of Sunday afternoon is a **part-time tutoring job paying ₹600**, attending the class costs him that **forgone ₹600**, besides the fee he pays.

questions.stem_md: Why does an economist usually find a smaller profit for an owner-run business than its accountant does? Explain briefly.
questions.solution_md: Implicit costs make the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: The accountant deducts only **explicit costs** (payments made). The economist also deducts **implicit costs**, the owner's **forgone salary, rent and interest** on his own factors. With more costs subtracted, **economic profit** is **smaller** than **accounting profit**.

marking_scheme.step: Economist: implicit costs too, so smaller profit

questions.stem_md: An imagined Kozhikode baker earns monthly revenue of ₹2,40,000 and pays explicit costs of ₹1,85,000. She could instead earn a salary of ₹40,000 and rent her shop out for ₹10,000. Calculate her accounting profit and economic profit, and say whether she should continue.
questions.solution_md: Two profits and a decision.

answer.model_answer_md: **Accounting profit** = ₹2,40,000 − ₹1,85,000 = **₹55,000**. Implicit costs = ₹40,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹50,000, so **economic profit** = ₹55,000 − ₹50,000 = **₹5,000**. As economic profit is **positive**, she earns more than in her best alternative and should **continue**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined engineer in Pune earns ₹90,000 a month in a job. She is thinking of leaving it to open a robotics workshop for school students in her own flat, which she could otherwise let for ₹25,000 a month. Explain opportunity cost and accounting cost in her situation, and evaluate what monthly accounting profit the workshop must earn before she should prefer it to her job.
questions.solution_md: Opportunity cost, accounting cost, implicit costs and the break-even accounting profit.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Opportunity cost** is the value of the **best alternative given up**. If she opens the workshop she gives up her **salary of ₹90,000** and the **rent of ₹25,000** from her flat.
2. **Accounting cost** would include only **payments** such as kits, a helper's wage and advertising; the forgone salary and rent are **not recorded**.
3. These forgone incomes are **implicit costs**, so **economic cost** = accounting cost + ₹1,15,000.
4. The workshop must earn an **accounting profit of at least ₹1,15,000** a month just to **match** her present position (zero economic profit).
5. **Judgement:** if she expects less than that, the job is the better choice on money terms; she might still prefer the workshop for **independence** or **future growth**, which opportunity cost in rupees does not capture.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following costs of an imagined Ludhiana cycle-parts factory is a fixed cost in the short run?

options.text_md: Insurance premium on the factory building
Payment for steel tubes used
Electricity used by the welding machines
Wages of workers paid per piece

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Insurance premium on the factory building. Insurance on the building must be paid whatever the output, even at zero output, so it is fixed. Steel, power for machines and piece wages rise with output, so they are variable.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Coimbatore textile mill shuts down for a week but keeps paying the watchman, rent and loan interest. During that week its total cost equals

options.text_md: zero
its total fixed cost
its total variable cost
its marginal cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** its total fixed cost. At zero output total variable cost is zero, so total cost equals total fixed cost, which must still be paid in the short run.

questions.stem_md: On a cost diagram for an imagined Surat diamond-cutting unit, the total variable cost curve

options.text_md: is a horizontal line above the output axis
starts from the level of fixed cost on the cost axis
starts from the origin and rises with output
falls continuously as output rises

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** starts from the origin and rises with output. With no output there is no variable cost, so TVC starts at the origin and rises as output grows; it is TC that starts at the TFC level, and TFC that is horizontal.

questions.stem_md: Why is the vertical distance between the total cost and total variable cost curves of an imagined Kota stone-polishing unit the same at every output?

options.text_md: The gap is marginal cost, which is constant
The gap is average cost, which is constant
Both curves are straight lines
The gap is total fixed cost, which does not change with output

questions.stem_md: With the help of described diagrams, explain the shapes of the TFC, TVC and TC curves and of the AFC curve for an imagined Kanpur leather-goods unit.
questions.solution_md: Four curves with reasons for their shapes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **TFC** is a **horizontal straight line**: fixed cost (rent, interest, salaried staff) stays the same at every output, even at zero.
2. **TVC** starts at the **origin**: no output, no variable cost. It rises first at a **decreasing rate** and then at an **increasing rate**, reflecting increasing and then diminishing returns to the variable factor.
3. **TC = TFC + TVC**: it has the **same shape as TVC** but starts at the **level of TFC** on the cost axis; the vertical gap between TC and TVC is constant and equals TFC.
4. **AFC = TFC ÷ Q** falls continuously, as fixed cost is spread over more output.
5. AFC is a **rectangular hyperbola**: it approaches the output axis but **never touches** it, since TFC is positive.

TC parallel to TVC from TFC

questions.stem_md: Explain why the short-run AVC and AC curves of an imagined Jalandhar sports-goods unit are U-shaped.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **AVC** first **falls** because, with fixed machinery, adding workers brings **increasing returns** to the variable factor; later diminishing returns make each unit **costlier**, so AVC **rises**: the **law of variable proportions**.
2. **AC = AFC + AVC**: at first both fall, so AC falls quickly.
3. Later the **rise in AVC outweighs the fall in AFC**, so AC also **rises**, giving a U-shape whose minimum lies to the right of AVC's.

AC rises once AVC's rise dominates

questions.solution_md: Ordered minima and the AC–AVC gap.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **AFC** (120 ÷ Q) falls continuously as a rectangular hyperbola.
2. **MC** falls to its **minimum at Q = 4** (12) and then rises; it is the first curve to turn up.
3. **AVC** falls while MC is below it and reaches its **minimum where MC cuts it**, at **Q = 6** (AVC = MC = 24).
4. **AC = AFC + AVC** keeps falling beyond Q = 6 because AFC is still falling; MC cuts **AC at its minimum** near **Q = 7.2**, to the **right** of AVC's minimum.
5. The **gap between AC and AVC** is AFC; it **narrows** as output rises but never closes. On the diagram all three of MC, AVC and AC are U-shaped, with MC rising through the lowest points of AVC and then AC.

marking_scheme.step: MC cuts AVC at its minimum (Q = 6)
MC cuts AC at its minimum, to the right
Gap between AC and AVC narrows

questions.stem_md: Explain, with a described diagram, why the long-run average cost curve of an imagined Ankleshwar chemicals firm is called an envelope curve. (Concepts only; no derivation.)

answer.model_answer_md:

2. In the long run the firm can choose the plant that gives the **lowest average cost** for any output it plans.
3. Joining these lowest points gives the **LAC**, which **touches each SAC from below** and **wraps around** the family of SAC curves, like an envelope. It is also called the **planning curve**.

questions.stem_md: Give reasons why the long-run average cost curve of an imagined Jamshedpur steel-pipe maker first falls and then rises, and contrast this with the reason for the U-shape of its short-run AVC.

answer.model_answer_md:

2. Beyond some size, **diseconomies of scale** (management becoming difficult, coordination costs) make LAC **rise**.
3. The short-run AVC is U-shaped for a different reason: the **law of variable proportions**, with plant size fixed and only the variable factor changing.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Nashik winery is deciding whether to stay with its present plant or build a larger one. Using the concepts of short-run and long-run cost curves, explain the choices it faces. (No derivation of the curves is required.)

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In the **short run** the winery's **plant is fixed**: its costs split into **fixed** (vats, building) and **variable** (grapes, bottles, labour).
2. Its **SAC curve** is **U-shaped** around the output the present plant suits; pushing far beyond it raises AVC because of **diminishing returns**.
3. In the **long run** it can choose any **plant size**: there are **no fixed costs**, and each plant size has its own SAC.
4. The **LAC** is the **envelope** of these SACs and shows the **lowest average cost** for each planned output.
5. If the winery plans an output much larger than its present plant suits, a **larger plant** gives a **lower point on the LAC**, so building it makes sense; for small increases, staying with the present plant may be cheaper.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain explicit, implicit, private and social costs, using an imagined Kozhikode bakery whose ovens' smoke troubles the neighbours.
(ii) The bakery's monthly revenue is ₹2,40,000 and its explicit costs are ₹1,85,000. The owner gives up a salary of ₹40,000 and rent of ₹10,000 on her shop. Calculate the accounting and economic profit and evaluate whether she has chosen well.
questions.solution_md: Four cost concepts; two profits and an evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Explicit costs** are **payments** to outsiders: flour, sugar, gas and the helpers' wages. **Implicit costs** are the **imputed value** of her own factors: the salary she gives up and the rent her shop could earn. **Private cost** is all the cost borne by the bakery itself, explicit and implicit. **Social cost** adds the **harm to the neighbours** from oven smoke, which the bakery does not pay for, so social cost **exceeds** private cost.
(ii) **Accounting profit** = ₹2,40,000 − ₹1,85,000 = **₹55,000**. Implicit costs = **₹50,000**, so **economic profit** = **₹5,000**. As this is positive, the bakery pays her more than her best alternative, so on money terms she has **chosen well**. The margin is **small**, however: a modest rise in costs or a fall in sales would wipe it out, and if smoke complaints led to a cleaner (costlier) oven, her economic profit could vanish.

questions.stem_md:

(ii) The **short-run AC** is a fairly **steep U** around the output the present kilns suit. It falls at first as **AFC** falls and the variable factor gives **increasing returns**, then rises as **diminishing returns** push AVC up, the **law of variable proportions**. The **long-run AC** is **flatter**, because the unit can build a bigger or smaller plant, and it **envelops** the short-run curves from below. Its U-shape comes from **economies** and then **diseconomies of scale**, not from fixed costs, which do not exist in the long run.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined cost sheet of a Khurja ceramic unit and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** AVC = 144 ÷ 6 = 24.

**(b)** MC = 175 − 144 = 31.

**(c) (i)** Compare MC and AVC either side of 6.

**OR (c) (ii)** AC values and the AFC effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **24**

**(b)** **31**

**(c) (i)** At output 5, MC = 13 is below AVC = 25, so AVC is **falling**; at output 7, MC = 31 is above AVC = 25, so AVC is **rising**. Hence AVC is **lowest at output 6** (24).

**OR (c) (ii)** AC6 = (120 + 144) ÷ 6 = **44**; AC7 = (120 + 175) ÷ 7 = **42.14**. AVC rises from 24 to 25, but **AFC falls** from 20 to 17.14; AC = AFC + AVC falls because the fall in AFC outweighs the rise in AVC.
